Title: 31K views · 99 reactions | We're closing the John Hart bridge again... just kidding 😜 

Now that we have your attention, we ARE closing a single southbound lane between the bridge and 5th Avenue as well as the right turn from Highway 97 onto 5th Avenue for eight days from August 11 to the morning of August 19.

The inside southbound lane and the two left turn lanes will remain open. Northbound lanes will not be impacted. Traffic will be slow going so expect delays, drive carefully around the work zone, and take an alternate route if possible. We appreciate your patience. 💙 

This is part of the wastewater project that we started last year. The project is coming to a close as we work to connect the new sanitary sewer line that runs underneath the bridge to the existing infrastructure. You can read more about this project on our website - link in the comments. | City of Prince George

[Have you seen this bad boy driving around the city? 🚗 We are completing our paved road condition assessment using advanced mobile LiDAR mapping technology! It's kind of like one of those google map cars, but specifically for roads. 🛣️ As it travels at normal traffic speeds, the system collects millions of georeferenced measurements and high-resolution images, creating a detailed 3D digital model of the road network in our community. The data is then analyzed to identify and measure pavement issues such as cracking, rutting, potholes, and other surface defects. It also provides information on roadway roughness and other indicators of pavement condition. Beyond pavement assessments, the LiDAR data can also be used for future analysis of roadway features such as pavement edges, lane markings, curbs, and other transportation assets. This gives us a valuable digital record of our road network that can support future asset management, maintenance, and infrastructure planning for our community. 😊 So, if you are out and about the next few days, keep your eyes peeled! 👀](https://www.google.com/100064728364513/videos/1597092632007794/?__so__=permalink&__cft__[0]=AZjiTpuZldTCTkIA5cHl7S9d0J5k_5d2ICQ3FAE8XhFYVoINULRmugS1nu1BCDpU3QF4FxhJBnCI2p0zz10JAxS144vWQOhIhvnh3cNSWUUT_kQZkirnropyhnepYZl7Q4N9A519mtYpDf-YAbFh_w)

Title: You Can Camp Beside Alberta’s Longest Vehicle Suspension Bridge
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5
HOT SUMMER GUIDE: Looking for a camping trip that offers more than the usual lake views? At Dunvegan Provincial Park, you can camp along the Peace River beside Alberta’s longest vehicle suspension bridge.
Alberta has no shortage of beautiful camping spots, but there aren’t many where the drive into your campground takes you across one of the province’s most impressive landmarks.
AtDunvegan Provincial Park, you can camp along the Peace River within view of the Dunvegan Bridge, Alberta’s longest vehicle suspension bridge. Surrounded by the rolling slopes of the Peace River Valley, the campground gives you easy access to riverside trails, an important provincial historic site, family-friendly attractions, and some seriously underrated northern Alberta scenery.
If you’re hoping to see a different side of the province this camping season, Dunvegan has everything you need for a road trip that combines history, scenery, and plenty of time outside.

### Camp Along the Mighty Peace River
Dunvegan Provincial Park is located approximately 26 kilometres south of Fairview on Highway 2, along the north shore of the Peace River.
The campground has 67 powered sites tucked among the valley slopes. Sites are lightly treed and include a mix of individual and double or shared sites, each with its own picnic table and fire pit. Alberta Parks also lists tap water, pit toilets, wheelchair-accessible washrooms, a playground, sewage disposal, firewood sales, and a payphone among the campground amenities.
It’s worth noting that the campground does not currently list showers, and all 67 campsites are powered. The campground is suitable for tents, trailers, and RVs, but campers should review individual site lengths and details before reserving.
For 2026, the camping season runs from May 14 to September 28, with reservable dates available through September 27. Reservations can be made up to 90 days before arrival throughAlberta Parks.
Once you’re set up, you can walk the campground and riverside trails, spend time beside the Peace River, or simply relax at your site and take in the surrounding valley. There are also opportunities for hiking, biking, fishing, canoeing, and kayaking in the park and nearby area.

### See Alberta’s Longest Vehicle Suspension Bridge
The Dunvegan Bridge carries Highway 2 across the Peace River and is the longest vehicle suspension bridge in Alberta. It opened in 1960, replacing the ferry service that had previously carried travellers between the two sides of the river.
Today, the bridge remains an important transportation link and one of the most recognizable landmarks in the Peace Country. Its bright yellow structure stands out against the river, surrounding hills, and green valley, making it well worth seeing from more than one angle.
You’ll get great views from around the campground and historic site, but you can also follow nearby trails for different perspectives over the river valley. The Maples Day Use Area, located west of the bridge, offers another place to picnic, walk, fish, or spend some time beside the water.
It’s a pretty impressive sight to wake up beside, especially when the morning light hits the bridge and the surrounding valley.

### Explore One of Northern Alberta’s Most Important Historic Sites
The bridge may be the first thing you notice, but Dunvegan’s history stretches back thousands of years.
The area is located on the traditional lands of the Tsattine, or Beaver, people and was an important gathering place long before European fur traders arrived.
In 1805, the North West Company established Fort Dunvegan as a fur-trading post. It became a Hudson’s Bay Company post in 1821, followed later by the establishment of Roman Catholic and Anglican missions. The valley was also home for a time to Henry Fuller “Twelve Foot” Davis, one of the Peace Country’s best-known historical figures.
Today,Historic Dunvegan is recognized as both a provincially and nationally designated historic resource. Visitors can explore four original, authentically restored and furnished buildings while learning about Indigenous history, the fur trade, and missionary life in the Peace River region.
The four buildings include the Revillon Frères trading post, St. Charles Mission Church and Rectory, and the Hudson’s Bay Company Factor’s House.
For the 2026 summer season, Historic Dunvegan is open from May 16 to September 7, Wednesday through Sunday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., as well as statutory holidays. Admission fees apply, so check the official website for current hours and visitor information before your trip.

### Visit Dunvegan Market Gardens
Right beside the provincial park isDunvegan Market Gardens, a family-owned business that has operated in the valley since 1953.
Depending on when you visit, you may find bedding plants, locally grown produce, berries, corn, pumpkins, locally made products, and seasonal activities. There’s also a licensed restaurant, ice cream, shopping, and mini golf.
It’s close enough to reach on a scenic riverside walk from the campground, making it a convenient place to grab something to eat or add a little extra entertainment to the day. Families can play a round of mini golf, pick up fresh produce, or stop for ice cream after exploring the trails and historic buildings.
Because its products and hours change throughout the growing season, check current information before visiting.
A view from above the Dunvegan Bridge that crosses the Peace River as part of Alberta Highway 2 between the Municipal District of Fairview No. Credit: Alberta Parks.

### A Different Kind of Alberta Camping Trip
Alberta is famous for mountain campgrounds, turquoise lakes, and Rocky Mountain views. Those places are incredible, but Dunvegan offers something completely different.
Here, you can wake up in the Peace River Valley, walk beneath Alberta’s longest vehicle suspension bridge, explore a place with thousands of years of history, and finish the day with locally grown food or a round of mini golf.

HOT SUMMER GUIDE: Looking for a camping trip that offers more than the usual lake views? At Dunvegan Provincial Park, you can camp along the Peace River beside Alberta’s longest vehicle suspension bridge.
Alberta has no shortage of beautiful camping spots, but there aren’t many where the drive into your campground takes you across one of the province’s most impressive landmarks.
AtDunvegan Provincial Park, you can camp along the Peace River within view of the Dunvegan Bridge, Alberta’s longest vehicle suspension bridge. Surrounded by the rolling slopes of the Peace River Valley, the campground gives you easy access to riverside trails, an important provincial historic site, family-friendly attractions, and some seriously underrated northern Alberta scenery.
If you’re hoping to see a different side of the province this camping season, Dunvegan has everything you need for a road trip that combines history, scenery, and plenty of time outside.
texts.1:
### Camp Along the Mighty Peace River
Dunvegan Provincial Park is located approximately 26 kilometres south of Fairview on Highway 2, along the north shore of the Peace River.
The campground has 67 powered sites tucked among the valley slopes. Sites are lightly treed and include a mix of individual and double or shared sites, each with its own picnic table and fire pit. Alberta Parks also lists tap water, pit toilets, wheelchair-accessible washrooms, a playground, sewage disposal, firewood sales, and a payphone among the campground amenities.
It’s worth noting that the campground does not currently list showers, and all 67 campsites are powered. The campground is suitable for tents, trailers, and RVs, but campers should review individual site lengths and details before reserving.
For 2026, the camping season runs from May 14 to September 28, with reservable dates available through September 27. Reservations can be made up to 90 days before arrival throughAlberta Parks.
Once you’re set up, you can walk the campground and riverside trails, spend time beside the Peace River, or simply relax at your site and take in the surrounding valley. There are also opportunities for hiking, biking, fishing, canoeing, and kayaking in the park and nearby area.
texts.2:
### See Alberta’s Longest Vehicle Suspension Bridge
The Dunvegan Bridge carries Highway 2 across the Peace River and is the longest vehicle suspension bridge in Alberta. It opened in 1960, replacing the ferry service that had previously carried travellers between the two sides of the river.
Today, the bridge remains an important transportation link and one of the most recognizable landmarks in the Peace Country. Its bright yellow structure stands out against the river, surrounding hills, and green valley, making it well worth seeing from more than one angle.
You’ll get great views from around the campground and historic site, but you can also follow nearby trails for different perspectives over the river valley. The Maples Day Use Area, located west of the bridge, offers another place to picnic, walk, fish, or spend some time beside the water.
It’s a pretty impressive sight to wake up beside, especially when the morning light hits the bridge and the surrounding valley.
texts.3:
### Explore One of Northern Alberta’s Most Important Historic Sites
The bridge may be the first thing you notice, but Dunvegan’s history stretches back thousands of years.
The area is located on the traditional lands of the Tsattine, or Beaver, people and was an important gathering place long before European fur traders arrived.
In 1805, the North West Company established Fort Dunvegan as a fur-trading post. It became a Hudson’s Bay Company post in 1821, followed later by the establishment of Roman Catholic and Anglican missions. The valley was also home for a time to Henry Fuller “Twelve Foot” Davis, one of the Peace Country’s best-known historical figures.
Today,Historic Dunvegan is recognized as both a provincially and nationally designated historic resource. Visitors can explore four original, authentically restored and furnished buildings while learning about Indigenous history, the fur trade, and missionary life in the Peace River region.
The four buildings include the Revillon Frères trading post, St. Charles Mission Church and Rectory, and the Hudson’s Bay Company Factor’s House.
For the 2026 summer season, Historic Dunvegan is open from May 16 to September 7, Wednesday through Sunday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., as well as statutory holidays. Admission fees apply, so check the official website for current hours and visitor information before your trip.
texts.4:
### Visit Dunvegan Market Gardens
Right beside the provincial park isDunvegan Market Gardens, a family-owned business that has operated in the valley since 1953.
Depending on when you visit, you may find bedding plants, locally grown produce, berries, corn, pumpkins, locally made products, and seasonal activities. There’s also a licensed restaurant, ice cream, shopping, and mini golf.
It’s close enough to reach on a scenic riverside walk from the campground, making it a convenient place to grab something to eat or add a little extra entertainment to the day. Families can play a round of mini golf, pick up fresh produce, or stop for ice cream after exploring the trails and historic buildings.
Because its products and hours change throughout the growing season, check current information before visiting.

[[](https://www.google.com/worldmatrixbydnyanesh) worldmatrixby... 12.9K This Town Lives Inside One Building Whittier, Alaska Explained There’s a place in the world where almost the entire town lives inside one building. No streets. No separate neighborhoods. Just one massive building where people live, work, and spend most of their lives. This place is Whittier, Alaska, and the building is called Begich Towers. Inside this building, you’ll find apartments, a school, a post office, a police station, grocery stores, offices, and even a church. People can do almost everything without stepping outside. Why? Because the weather here is extreme. Winters are brutally cold, with heavy snowfall, strong winds, and freezing temperatures that can last for months. The town is also very isolated — there’s only one road connecting it to the outside world. That’s why nearly 90% of Whittier’s population lives inside this single building. It’s not just a building… it’s an entire self-contained town under one roof. [[](https://www.google.com/jeweladdisonofficial) jeweladdisono... 2,118 People love quoting Alaska’s crime statistics. Usually the loudest voices… have never actually lived here. And before anyone jumps in the comments Yes. I’ve read the statistics too. But I’ve also lived here my entire life. So I’ve seen something the data can’t always show. Real life. And don’t get me wrong. If you or someone you love has been directly affected by crime that experience is real and it matters. But when people considering a move ask me what it actually feels like living here… most locals will tell you the same thing. It feels a lot safer than the numbers make it sound. Here’s why the stats can be misleading: 1️⃣ Alaska’s crime rate is measured per capita Which means incidents are compared to population size. And Alaska has a very small population spread across a massive state. So even a relatively small number of incidents can make the rate look higher than it actually feels day to day. 2️⃣ Safety here is extremely location specific Just like anywhere else. Neighborhood, community, lifestyle all play a huge role in your experience. 3️⃣ The culture here is different A lot of communities are tight knit. People know their neighbors. People watch out for each other. It’s not uncommon to take a walk in the evening and feel completely at peace. Most people who’ve actually lived here talk more about the privacy, quiet, and freedom they feel… not fear. I’ve lived in multiple parts of Alaska and now live in Fairbanks. It’s the second largest city in the state but still somehow feels like a small town. Restaurants. Box stores. Local boutiques. Hospital. International airport. Yet only about 35,000 people in the city and around 95,000 in the entire borough. So if you’re one of the people wondering what life here is really like… and you want help understanding where people actually choose to live in Fairbanks Comment “GUIDE” and I’ll send you my Guide to Fairbanks’ Most Popular Neighborhoods. # Yukon Suspension Bridge & Summit Tour
The Yukon Suspension Bridge & Summit Tour is especially formatted for those who want to experience and photograph the incredible beauty of the White Pass and Canada's Boreal forest. The Yukon Suspension Bridge & Summit Tour will introduce you to Skagway's rich Klondike Gold Rush history and unbelievable wilderness. Journey through the Tormented Valley and past Fraser Station! This Skagway tour is ideal for travelers wishing to explore the beauty of the Alaskan and Canadian Wilderness.

The Delaware River Joint Toll Bridge Commission says the Washington Crossing Bridge is suffering from major structural, operational and safety problems as officials begin deciding what should happen to the 120-year-old span. In a newly released video, the commission outlined long-standing issues with the toll-free bridge that links Mercer County, New Jersey and Bucks County, Pennsylvania. The bridge was built in 1905, predates modern automobile traffic and now has narrow 7.5-foot travel lanes, limited load capacity, frequent vehicle strikes and aging foundations. The video is part of a multi-year “Washington Crossing Bridge Alternatives Analysis,” launched in August 2024, to study options for improving safety, mobility and pedestrian access while protecting nearby businesses. Officials must also decide whether revenue from the commission’s toll bridges should be used to fund major work on the aging structure. opened.anchor: End of the road for cars on Kalemouth Suspension Bridge
opened.information:
Source: https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-scotland-south-scotland-67566267
Title: End of the road for cars on Kalemouth Suspension Bridge
Chunks: 0,1
5 December 2023
Giancarlo Rinaldi South Scotland reporter, BBC Scotland news website
Alan Reid
Vehicles were last allowed to cross the bridge more than three years ago
**A report has concluded it would not be "value for money" to let cars back on a historic Borders bridge.**
The Kalemouth Suspension Bridge - built in the 1830s - was shut to vehicles in August 2020 after "substantial decay" was found in its timber deck.
Further investigations saw pedestrian numbers limited to 10 at a time.
The council has agreed to carrying out work to lift that restriction but decided spending £4m to allow cars to use it again could not be justified.
The bridge near Eckford was designed and built by Capt Samuel Brown who also built the Union Chain Bridge linking Scotland and England.
*   Bridge linking Scotland and England reopens  
*   In pictures: The restoration of the Union Chain Bridge
It carries an unclassified road over the River Teviot and, prior to its closure, allowed single-file traffic - weighing less than three tonnes - to cross between the A698 and about 12 properties in Ormiston Mains.
Tests undertaken a little over three years ago found the category A listed structure no longer demonstrated "sufficient strength" to cope with such loads.
PA Media
The cost of fully reopening the Union Chain Bridge - about twice the size of Kalemouth - was about £10.5m
It has meant people living in the small settlement nearby have had to take alternative routes - the maximum diversion being seven miles (11km).
A full refurbishment of the Union Chain Bridge cost about £10.5m and Scottish Borders Council (SBC) estimates that a similar project at Kalemouth - which is about half the span - would cost about £4m.
It said that made the scheme "cost prohibitive".
Instead, it has agreed to renew the timber elements to allow it to be safely used by pedestrians and cyclists only.
Jim Barton
The bridge was built in the 1830s
However, the council currently has a capital budget of just £750,000-a-year allocated to bridge improvement work across its entire network of about 1,200 bridges.
It is hoped that it can secure some external funding towards the £1m cost of the Kalemouth work.

A report to the local authority's executive committee warned that failure to carry out the upgrade could force the bridge to shut completely.
It also warned that it was difficult to estimate exact costs at the design stage and they could ultimately exceed £1m.
One regular bridge user, who did not wish to be named, told the BBC that the situation caused significant problems for residents.
"The permanent closure of the bridge at Eckford is a huge inconvenience to residents and visitors," she said.
"The extra miles that they have to divert and travel is hardly great for climate change.
"It is ridiculous that a so-called major country cannot find a way to do basic repairs."
Alan Reid
Prior to August 2020, vehicles up to three tonnes could cross the bridge

Title: The Very Modern Historic Bridge
Chunks: 0,1
_The Brooklyn Bridge, conceived by_**John Roebling**_, is a combination of cable-stayed and suspension bridge technologies._
[click to read]
After many long years of planning and building, along with numerous setbacks, the Brooklyn Bridge opened to traffic on May 24, 1883. The first vehicle to cross the bridge was **Emily Roebling**’s horse-drawn carriage. Emily carried with her a rooster in a cage symbolic of the victory realized that day. The victory was wrought from the darkness of the bridge’s deep underwater foundations, now realized in the vast structure that towered in the light traversing the river. As Emily gazed up at the bridge’s great gothic arches, which resembled the windows of a mighty cathedral, she reflected on her 11-year struggle, carrying a torch passed to her from her father-in-law, **John Roebling**, and her husband, **Washington Roebling**. Before the Brooklyn Bridge could come to symbolize a mighty American city, it had to begin with the vision of one man.
**John Augustus Roebling** was born (Johann August Röbling) on June 12, 1806, in Mühlhausen, in the Kingdom of Prussia (now part of Germany). His mother saw that he was somewhat of a _“wunderkind” (child prodigy)_ and sought out education for him in math and science at a young age.
He sat for the surveyor’s examination at 18 and then attended the _Bauakademie (Building Academy)_ in Berlin. At 19, he obtained a job designing and supervising the construction of military roads. During this time, he actually sketched the concept for several suspension bridges, though they were never built. At the time, suspension bridges were built with large chain links fastened together to hold up the roadway. These chain suspenders sometimes failed, but Roebling was still fascinated by them.

Leaving government service in 1828, he returned home to study for his engineer’s exam; he never took it. Instead, he made plans to come to America. Roebling and his brother Carl purchased 1,582 acres of land in Butler County, Pennsylvania. They called their settlement Germania and took up farming. Eventually the settlement, near Pittsburgh, came to be known as Saxonburg. Roebling struggled as a farmer, however, and as canals and railroads were being built throughout western Pennsylvania, he found ready work as an engineer.
The Allegheny Mountains stood in the way of a direct water connection between Philadelphia and Pittsburg. The canal designers, rather than spending years building locks or tunnels, decided to build a portage railway. Canal boats would be carried on large rail carriages across the high mountain terrain. The weak link in this system was the hemp rope used to tow them. It would often snap with disastrous results. Roebling thought he had a better idea. In his shop behind the town church, he experimented with weaving rope from steel wire. The tensile strength of his _“wire rope”_ far exceeded that of hemp.
The wire rope was a boon to the canal operators, who regularly had to replace the hemp. Not only was it important to canal operators, but it proved to be a superior material for suspension bridges as well. Some of Roebling’s first suspension bridges actually carried canal boats across aqueducts—a technology made possible by the properties of his woven wire. In fact, the oldest steel-wire suspension bridge in the United States is Roebling’s Delaware Aqueduct. It was opened in 1849 to carry the channel of the Delaware and Hudson Canal water across the Delaware River. It has since been converted into a highway bridge.
In 1848, Roebling moved his wire-making operation to Trenton, New Jersey, where he built a huge factory complex. He built an enormous suspension bridge with two levels—one for vehicles and one for trains—across the Niagara Gorge to carry traffic between New York and Canada. Roebling’s son Washington joined his father in 1858 and became his business partner. John Roebling was an exacting taskmaster, not an easy man to please, but when Washington married**Emily Warren**in 1865, the brilliant young woman won her father-in-law’s heart.(read more)

The weak link in this system was the hemp rope used to tow them. It would often snap with disastrous results. Roebling thought he had a better idea. In his shop behind the town church, he experimented with weaving rope from steel wire. The tensile strength of his _“wire rope”_ far exceeded that of hemp.
The wire rope was a boon to the canal operators, who regularly had to replace the hemp. Not only was it important to canal operators, but it proved to be a superior material for suspension bridges as well. Some of Roebling’s first suspension bridges actually carried canal boats across aqueducts—a technology made possible by the properties of his woven wire. In fact, the oldest steel-wire suspension bridge in the United States is Roebling’s Delaware Aqueduct. It was opened in 1849 to carry the channel of the Delaware and Hudson Canal water across the Delaware River. It has since been converted into a highway bridge.
In 1848, Roebling moved his wire-making operation to Trenton, New Jersey, where he built a huge factory complex. He built an enormous suspension bridge with two levels—one for vehicles and one for trains—across the Niagara Gorge to carry traffic between New York and Canada. Roebling’s son Washington joined his father in 1858 and became his business partner. John Roebling was an exacting taskmaster, not an easy man to please, but when Washington married**Emily Warren**in 1865, the brilliant young woman won her father-in-law’s heart.(read more)

Located at One Collins Diboll Circle in City Park, the New Orleans Museum of Art is easy to find. Arrive by car, bike, bus or streetcar. Ample free parking is available in front of NOMA on Lelong Drive or behind the Besthoff Sculpture Garden.

## By Car
### From I-10 West/Baton Rouge
Take Exit 231A toward City Park/Metairie Road.
Turn left onto City Park Ave away from Metairie Road. Continue down City Park Avenue past Canal and Delgado Community College. Turn left onto N. Carrollton Ave from City Park Avenue. Turn left at Esplanade Avenue. You are facing Lelong Drive and NOMA.

## By Car
### From I-10 East/Downtown
Take the Carrollton Ave North, Exit 232, toward US-61/Tulane Avenue. Merge onto S. Carrollton Avenue. Continue 1.6 miles. Turn left at Esplanade Avenue. You are facing Lelong Drive and NOMA.

## By Car
### Parking
Parking is always free on Lelong Drive and the streets surrounding NOMA within City Park. Handicap spaces are reserved at the front of the museum adjacent an entrance ramp. The handicap entrances are located on the left and right side of the museum near Café NOMA and the NOMA Museum Shop. Ramps at the main museum entrance stairs lead to a courtyard. Ring the buzzer on the door and security staff will allow entry. Please call 504.658.4105 if you require additional assistance.

## By Taxi or Ride Share
It will take about 15 minutes to arrive at NOMA by cab, Lyft, or Uber from the French Quarter or CBD. Click here for more information about local cab companies.

## By Bike
NOMA is less than 3 miles from downtown and the historic French Quarter. Blue Bikes—New Orleans’ community-run bikeshare—provides stations across the city. Lock up at the two conveniently located hubs near the museum at City Park and Esplanade Avenues or at Café du Monde.

## By Streetcar
The Canal–City Park streetcar lineterminates at the intersection of Wisner Avenue and Esplanade Street, within a short walking distance of NOMA and the Besthoff Sculpture Garden. Click here for the streetcar schedule.

## By Bus
Buses and streetcars are operated by the New Orleans Regional Transit Authority. RTA bus routes with stops near the museum include #27-Louisiana, #60-Hayne, #90 Carrollton, and #91 Jackson-Esplanade. Visit the RTA website for route maps and schedules.
_Visitors from across the state of Louisiana receive $3 off one adult general museum admission ticket when they show their same-day ticket or receipt fromNew Orleans Regional Transit Authoritybuses or streetcars or from theBlue Bikesrideshare network._

Serving as the grand entrance to City Park since its establishment in 1911, this fine-arts museum exudes the elegance of classic Greek architecture. With the addition of modern wings, NOMA blends old-world charm with contemporary spaciousness, featuring nearly fifty galleries that house a remarkable permanent collection, including nearly 40,000 objects spanning various historical periods.
The permanent collection features an array of American and European art, with a strong emphasis on French works, including pieces by renowned artists such as Monet, Renoir, Rodin, Matisse, Picasso, Cornell, and Pollock. Notably, NOMA also showcases the talents of Louisiana artists and offers a diverse selection of art forms, including photography, ceramics, and glassworks from cultures worldwide. The museum takes pride in its significant holdings of African, pre-Columbian, and Asian art.
In addition to its permanent collection, NOMA hosts a year-round schedule of traveling exhibitions, special events, guided tours, and public programs.
Tip:
Visitors should not miss the Sydney and Walda Besthoff Sculpture Garden, a beautifully landscaped 5-acre area situated behind the main building. This gated garden showcases fifty modern sculptures nestled among lush foliage, lagoons, walking trails, and picturesque bridges. The museum complex also features amenities such as a gift shop, a small theater for film screenings, and the newly renovated Café NOMA by Ralph Brennan, offering a delectable array of artisanal flatbreads, sandwiches, salads, veggie bowls, freshly baked breads, and sweets.

## What NOMA Actually Is
The New Orleans Museum of Art is the oldest fine arts museum in the city, and one of the most quietly impressive art institutions in the American South. It was founded in 1910 and formally opened on December 16, 1911, as the Delgado Museum of Art, named for its founding benefactor Isaac Delgado, a sugar broker who donated the funds for the original building. It opened with just nine works on display. Today, the permanent collection numbers more than 40,000 accessioned works and spans 5,000 years of human creativity.
The collection's depth is worth understanding before you arrive. NOMA has historically strong holdings in French and American decorative arts, photography, glass, African art, and Japanese works. It is not a survey museum trying to cover everything superficially. If you go in knowing where its strengths lie, you will get significantly more out of the visit than someone who wanders room to room without a plan.
💡 Local tip
Louisiana residents get free museum admission every Wednesday through The Helis Foundation's Art for All initiative. The Besthoff Sculpture Garden is always free for everyone, regardless of residency or day of the week.

## The Building and Its Setting
NOMA's original Beaux-Arts building, designed by architect James Freret, sits at the end of an oak-canopied approach inside City Park, one of the largest urban parks in the United States. The formal entrance is on Collins Diboll Circle, and the symmetry of the facade, the shallow steps, and the surrounding moss-draped trees create an arrival sequence that feels genuinely different from the rest of New Orleans. You are no longer in the French Quarter's narrow streets or the Garden District's residential calm. This corner of Mid-City has a campus quality.
The museum has expanded significantly since 1911, with later wings adding gallery space without visually overwhelming the original structure. The institution sits within City Park, which means a visit to NOMA pairs naturally with a longer afternoon in the park itself, whether that means the botanical garden, the lagoons, or simply a long walk under the ancient live oaks.

## The Sydney and Walda Besthoff Sculpture Garden
The eleven-acre sculpture garden (or twelve-acre according to recent updates) adjacent to the museum is the part of NOMA that consistently surprises first-time visitors. It is free to enter, open to the public, and contains more than 90 sculptures by major figures in 20th and 21st century art. The works are arranged throughout a landscape of lagoons, bridges, and mature trees, which means you are moving through art the way you move through a park rather than a gallery.
The setting rewards slow walking. Sculptures by artists including George Segal, Henry Moore, and Louise Bourgeois appear around corners and across water reflections in ways that feel genuinely considered rather than incidental. The garden is one of the better photography locations in all of New Orleans, and it does not require any tickets, reservations, or museum entry. For a full list of other photography-worthy spots around the city, the most Instagrammable spots in New Orleans guide is worth a look before your visit.
Morning light, particularly in spring and fall, falls across the lagoon at an angle that makes the garden feel almost theatrical. By midday, especially in summer, the lack of shade in parts of the garden becomes noticeable. If you are sensitive to heat, the garden works better as a first stop before the museum rather than after.

## How the Visit Unfolds by Time of Day
NOMA opens at 10 am Tuesday through Sunday, but closes on Mondays. Wednesday hours extend to 7 pm, which is the only evening slot available. On a typical weekday morning shortly after opening, the museum is genuinely quiet. The galleries on the upper floors, particularly those devoted to photography and glass, are often empty for stretches of time. If you want to spend real time in front of individual works without other visitors in your field of view, Tuesday and Thursday mornings are consistently the calmest.
Weekend afternoons bring more families and larger groups, particularly to the ground-floor galleries and the gift shop area. The sculpture garden fills somewhat on weekend mornings when the weather is mild, but it almost never feels crowded in the way that Jackson Square or Bourbon Street do. Even on a busy Saturday, the scale of the outdoor space absorbs visitors without the place feeling overrun.
⚠️ What to skip
Monday closures catch visitors off guard. If your trip to New Orleans is short, check the weekly calendar at noma.org before planning a Museum Day. Wednesday evenings until 7 pm are a useful option for travelers with packed daytime itineraries.

## Getting There
NOMA sits at the far end of City Park, accessible from the intersection of Carrollton Avenue and Esplanade Avenue. The Canal Street streetcar line runs to City Park and deposits you within walking distance of the museum entrance, making it possible to reach the museum from the French Quarter without a car or rideshare. The walk through the park from the streetcar stop is pleasant and adds to the overall experience.
Rideshare via Uber or Lyft is straightforward and drops you at the museum entrance directly. If you are combining NOMA with the New Orleans Botanical Garden or the Besthoff Sculpture Garden, a half-day built around the City Park complex is entirely practical. Parking is available within City Park if you are driving.

## The Permanent Collection: Where to Focus
With more than 40,000 accessioned works, NOMA's permanent collection is large enough that trying to see everything in one visit produces fatigue rather than appreciation. The photography collection is one of the museum's most recognized strengths, covering the medium from its 19th-century origins through contemporary practice. The glass collection, which includes European and American decorative glass as well as studio glass, is frequently cited as one of the finest of its kind in the South.
The African art galleries and the Japanese holdings are worth seeking out if those areas interest you. They are not trophy collections assembled for prestige. They reflect decades of focused acquisition and have genuine curatorial depth. The French art holdings tie directly into New Orleans' history as a French colonial city and provide interesting context for the broader cultural narrative of the region.
If you are building a broader understanding of New Orleans' history alongside your museum visit, the New Orleans history guide provides useful context for the city's French and Creole heritage that shows up throughout NOMA's collection.

## Who Should Think Twice
NOMA is not the right fit for every traveler in every mood. If you have only one day in New Orleans and your priority is live music, street food, and neighborhood atmosphere, the time investment of a museum visit in City Park may not be the best use of your afternoon. The museum is also a real museum in the traditional sense: it rewards patience, reading, and unhurried movement through galleries. Visitors expecting interactive exhibits or immersive entertainment will find it more conventional than they hoped.
The mid-summer heat makes the sculpture garden uncomfortable for extended outdoor browsing between roughly 11 am and 3 pm. If you are visiting in July or August, plan the outdoor component for early morning or late afternoon. The museum's air conditioning makes the indoor galleries a genuinely pleasant escape from the heat during those months, which is itself a practical reason to visit.

## Insider Tips
*   The upper floors of the museum receive the fewest visitors even on busy days. If you want near-solitude with the photography or glass collections, go upstairs first rather than following the crowd through the ground-floor galleries.  
*   Wednesday evenings until 7 pm are underused by tourists. If you want the museum mostly to yourself and do not qualify for the Louisiana residents' free admission, a Wednesday evening visit still gets you past the crowds.  
*   The sculpture garden's lagoon reflects the surrounding oaks and sculpture most clearly in the early morning, before wind picks up. If you care about photography, arrive before 10 am when the garden opens with the museum.  
*   NOMA's gift shop has a notably good selection of art books focused on New Orleans, Louisiana, and Southern art history. It is worth browsing even if you are not a regular museum shop visitor.  
*   Combining NOMA with the adjacent New Orleans Botanical Garden and a walk through the broader City Park grounds makes for a full day that stays entirely within one neighborhood and costs very little.

NOMA is less than 3 miles from downtown and the historic French Quarter. Blue Bikes—New Orleans’ community-run bikeshare—provides stations across the city. Lock up at the two conveniently located hubs near the museum at City Park and Esplanade Avenues or at Café du Monde.
texts.6:
## By Streetcar
The Canal–City Park streetcar lineterminates at the intersection of Wisner Avenue and Esplanade Street, within a short walking distance of NOMA and the Besthoff Sculpture Garden. Click here for the streetcar schedule.
texts.7:
## By Bus
Buses and streetcars are operated by the New Orleans Regional Transit Authority. RTA bus routes with stops near the museum include #27-Louisiana, #60-Hayne, #90 Carrollton, and #91 Jackson-Esplanade. Visit the RTA website for route maps and schedules.
_Visitors from across the state of Louisiana receive $3 off one adult general museum admission ticket when they show their same-day ticket or receipt fromNew Orleans Regional Transit Authoritybuses or streetcars or from theBlue Bikesrideshare network._

Serving as the grand entrance to City Park since its establishment in 1911, this fine-arts museum exudes the elegance of classic Greek architecture. With the addition of modern wings, NOMA blends old-world charm with contemporary spaciousness, featuring nearly fifty galleries that house a remarkable permanent collection, including nearly 40,000 objects spanning various historical periods.
The permanent collection features an array of American and European art, with a strong emphasis on French works, including pieces by renowned artists such as Monet, Renoir, Rodin, Matisse, Picasso, Cornell, and Pollock. Notably, NOMA also showcases the talents of Louisiana artists and offers a diverse selection of art forms, including photography, ceramics, and glassworks from cultures worldwide. The museum takes pride in its significant holdings of African, pre-Columbian, and Asian art.
In addition to its permanent collection, NOMA hosts a year-round schedule of traveling exhibitions, special events, guided tours, and public programs.
Tip:
Visitors should not miss the Sydney and Walda Besthoff Sculpture Garden, a beautifully landscaped 5-acre area situated behind the main building. This gated garden showcases fifty modern sculptures nestled among lush foliage, lagoons, walking trails, and picturesque bridges. The museum complex also features amenities such as a gift shop, a small theater for film screenings, and the newly renovated Café NOMA by Ralph Brennan, offering a delectable array of artisanal flatbreads, sandwiches, salads, veggie bowls, freshly baked breads, and sweets.

## What NOMA Actually Is
The New Orleans Museum of Art is the oldest fine arts museum in the city, and one of the most quietly impressive art institutions in the American South. It was founded in 1910 and formally opened on December 16, 1911, as the Delgado Museum of Art, named for its founding benefactor Isaac Delgado, a sugar broker who donated the funds for the original building. It opened with just nine works on display. Today, the permanent collection numbers more than 40,000 accessioned works and spans 5,000 years of human creativity.
The collection's depth is worth understanding before you arrive. NOMA has historically strong holdings in French and American decorative arts, photography, glass, African art, and Japanese works. It is not a survey museum trying to cover everything superficially. If you go in knowing where its strengths lie, you will get significantly more out of the visit than someone who wanders room to room without a plan.
💡 Local tip
Louisiana residents get free museum admission every Wednesday through The Helis Foundation's Art for All initiative. The Besthoff Sculpture Garden is always free for everyone, regardless of residency or day of the week.
texts.1:
## The Building and Its Setting
NOMA's original Beaux-Arts building, designed by architect James Freret, sits at the end of an oak-canopied approach inside City Park, one of the largest urban parks in the United States. The formal entrance is on Collins Diboll Circle, and the symmetry of the facade, the shallow steps, and the surrounding moss-draped trees create an arrival sequence that feels genuinely different from the rest of New Orleans. You are no longer in the French Quarter's narrow streets or the Garden District's residential calm. This corner of Mid-City has a campus quality.
The museum has expanded significantly since 1911, with later wings adding gallery space without visually overwhelming the original structure. The institution sits within City Park, which means a visit to NOMA pairs naturally with a longer afternoon in the park itself, whether that means the botanical garden, the lagoons, or simply a long walk under the ancient live oaks.

## The Sydney and Walda Besthoff Sculpture Garden
The eleven-acre sculpture garden (or twelve-acre according to recent updates) adjacent to the museum is the part of NOMA that consistently surprises first-time visitors. It is free to enter, open to the public, and contains more than 90 sculptures by major figures in 20th and 21st century art. The works are arranged throughout a landscape of lagoons, bridges, and mature trees, which means you are moving through art the way you move through a park rather than a gallery.
The setting rewards slow walking. Sculptures by artists including George Segal, Henry Moore, and Louise Bourgeois appear around corners and across water reflections in ways that feel genuinely considered rather than incidental. The garden is one of the better photography locations in all of New Orleans, and it does not require any tickets, reservations, or museum entry. For a full list of other photography-worthy spots around the city, the most Instagrammable spots in New Orleans guide is worth a look before your visit.
Morning light, particularly in spring and fall, falls across the lagoon at an angle that makes the garden feel almost theatrical. By midday, especially in summer, the lack of shade in parts of the garden becomes noticeable. If you are sensitive to heat, the garden works better as a first stop before the museum rather than after.
texts.4:
## How the Visit Unfolds by Time of Day
NOMA opens at 10 am Tuesday through Sunday, but closes on Mondays. Wednesday hours extend to 7 pm, which is the only evening slot available. On a typical weekday morning shortly after opening, the museum is genuinely quiet. The galleries on the upper floors, particularly those devoted to photography and glass, are often empty for stretches of time. If you want to spend real time in front of individual works without other visitors in your field of view, Tuesday and Thursday mornings are consistently the calmest.
Weekend afternoons bring more families and larger groups, particularly to the ground-floor galleries and the gift shop area. The sculpture garden fills somewhat on weekend mornings when the weather is mild, but it almost never feels crowded in the way that Jackson Square or Bourbon Street do. Even on a busy Saturday, the scale of the outdoor space absorbs visitors without the place feeling overrun.
⚠️ What to skip
Monday closures catch visitors off guard. If your trip to New Orleans is short, check the weekly calendar at noma.org before planning a Museum Day. Wednesday evenings until 7 pm are a useful option for travelers with packed daytime itineraries.
texts.5:
## Getting There
NOMA sits at the far end of City Park, accessible from the intersection of Carrollton Avenue and Esplanade Avenue. The Canal Street streetcar line runs to City Park and deposits you within walking distance of the museum entrance, making it possible to reach the museum from the French Quarter without a car or rideshare. The walk through the park from the streetcar stop is pleasant and adds to the overall experience.
Rideshare via Uber or Lyft is straightforward and drops you at the museum entrance directly. If you are combining NOMA with the New Orleans Botanical Garden or the Besthoff Sculpture Garden, a half-day built around the City Park complex is entirely practical. Parking is available within City Park if you are driving.
texts.6:
## The Permanent Collection: Where to Focus
With more than 40,000 accessioned works, NOMA's permanent collection is large enough that trying to see everything in one visit produces fatigue rather than appreciation. The photography collection is one of the museum's most recognized strengths, covering the medium from its 19th-century origins through contemporary practice. The glass collection, which includes European and American decorative glass as well as studio glass, is frequently cited as one of the finest of its kind in the South.
The African art galleries and the Japanese holdings are worth seeking out if those areas interest you. They are not trophy collections assembled for prestige. They reflect decades of focused acquisition and have genuine curatorial depth. The French art holdings tie directly into New Orleans' history as a French colonial city and provide interesting context for the broader cultural narrative of the region.
If you are building a broader understanding of New Orleans' history alongside your museum visit, the New Orleans history guide provides useful context for the city's French and Creole heritage that shows up throughout NOMA's collection.
texts.7:
## Who Should Think Twice
NOMA is not the right fit for every traveler in every mood. If you have only one day in New Orleans and your priority is live music, street food, and neighborhood atmosphere, the time investment of a museum visit in City Park may not be the best use of your afternoon. The museum is also a real museum in the traditional sense: it rewards patience, reading, and unhurried movement through galleries. Visitors expecting interactive exhibits or immersive entertainment will find it more conventional than they hoped.
The mid-summer heat makes the sculpture garden uncomfortable for extended outdoor browsing between roughly 11 am and 3 pm. If you are visiting in July or August, plan the outdoor component for early morning or late afternoon. The museum's air conditioning makes the indoor galleries a genuinely pleasant escape from the heat during those months, which is itself a practical reason to visit.
texts.8:
## Insider Tips
*   The upper floors of the museum receive the fewest visitors even on busy days. If you want near-solitude with the photography or glass collections, go upstairs first rather than following the crowd through the ground-floor galleries.  
*   Wednesday evenings until 7 pm are underused by tourists. If you want the museum mostly to yourself and do not qualify for the Louisiana residents' free admission, a Wednesday evening visit still gets you past the crowds.  
*   The sculpture garden's lagoon reflects the surrounding oaks and sculpture most clearly in the early morning, before wind picks up. If you care about photography, arrive before 10 am when the garden opens with the museum.  
*   NOMA's gift shop has a notably good selection of art books focused on New Orleans, Louisiana, and Southern art history. It is worth browsing even if you are not a regular museum shop visitor.  
*   Combining NOMA with the adjacent New Orleans Botanical Garden and a walk through the broader City Park grounds makes for a full day that stays entirely within one neighborhood and costs very little.

[[](https://www.instagram.com/whatrvdoing) whatrvdoing 6,329 Golden Skybridge in British Columbia is home to Canada’s highest suspension bridges, and the views are honestly unreal. Mountains, waterfalls, and forest in every direction..it’s one of those places where you just stop and stare for a minute. Now for the honesty: I’m scared of heights 😅 I almost didn’t do this… but I did, and I’m so glad I pushed past the fear. Shaky legs and all, it was 100% worth it. # Bc Suspension Bridge
## golden bc suspension bridge
[[](https://www.instagram.com/msrachelteodoro) msrachelteodoro 3,711 Wondering (like us) if it is still worth it to visit the Capilano Suspension Bridge even in the rain? We already pre booked tickets and the weather wasn’t looking great. But we decided to go anyway. After our visit we were soaked completely but we would have still gone again in the rain. Here’s why…and a few things we’d do to prepare differently. @capilanosuspensionbridge is one of the MAJOR tourist attractions in Vancouver and it’s expensive! As a traveler who is mindful of big purchases I want the most bang for my buck. And honestly, a rainy winter day gave us that. There were hardly any people and I know we’ve all seen photos of crowded bridges and wall to wall people, and if you ask me, that kind of makes a magical trip in the forest seem a bit less magical. I like less crowds, and I think this was the winning combination! But after a few hours we were completely soaked through. Here are some tips: ☔️wear waterproof clothing! We didn’t plan appropriately and wish we had worn waterproof pants and shoes. Despite our waterproof coats, we still got soaked through. ☔️prepare to get wet! This is a rainforest setting. Embrace it. Attitude is everything! ☔️bring a change of clothes. We stayed the weekend in Vancouver so we were glad we had clothes to change into after our walk. Because there are less crowds, you will likely spend less time. You’ve got less time waiting to chat with the wildlife specialists throughout the park, less time waiting for a less crowded photo, less time walking around because you’re dodging crowds. If you don’t mind getting a little wet, I say go for it! The moodiness of the rain makes the walk through the forest that much more magical! Have you visited the Capilano Bridge before? Would you go in the rain? #familytravelblogger #capilanosuspensionbridge #vancouver #visitvancouver #thingstodovancouver](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DUeOi6EkuEe/?utm_source=popular_topic_grid)

[[](https://www.instagram.com/snoot_adventures) snoot_adventures 13.7K ⚠️The truth about visiting Capilano Suspension Bridge Park (pet friendly park). - Although there is staff at both ends of the bridge that is supposed to monitor the amount of people on the bridge at the same time, nobody in my group felt like this was being done properly. The bridge was insane packed, and it was extremely anxiety inducing because you’re squished from all sides. There is no way to get off the bridge until the people in front of you have moved forward, so you are virtually stuck and at the mercy of the other hundred people on the bridge with you (not exaggerating). This personally made me feel very unsafe. - Although this park is technically pet friendly, I would not attempt it with a dog unless the dog is either small enough to be carried in a backpack (you will need both hands free to cross the bridge safely) or you know for a fact that your dog is comfortable walking on super shaky/wobbly surfaces where you can clearly see the drop below. I saw several terrified pet dogs being dragged by their owners - please just don’t 💔 - Because of the amount of people on the bridge at the same time, nobody is looking where they are stepping - everyone is just trying to hold on to the railings for dear life to not fall because it shakes so much. So if you have a dog with you, you’re going to have to be good at body blocking and protecting your dog so he doesn’t get trampled. People can fall on you/your dog due to how shaky the bridge is (your dog can loose balance too). For us we managed by staying in between people we knew so that at least I knew we were safe in front and behind, so I could focus on blocking the side. - The fact that this park is pet friendly also means that you may be stuck on the bridge with a random dog in your dog’s face. Unfortunately, I saw very irresponsible people bring a reactive dog (not friendly) into the park - scary stuff. - The main suspension bridge is very long, shakes like crazy, and not accessible to anyone with mobility issues or using mobility devices such as a wheelchair. There is no other way to get into the park than to cross that suspension bridge.

[[](https://www.instagram.com/techbehindthings) techbehindthings 992K 🤷How the Suspension Bridge Was Invented. Every massive bridge, from the Golden Gate to the Akashi Kaikyo, is built on simple physics: the Catenary Curve! You can reinvent the suspension bridge in a few easy steps: 1. The Catenary Curve The Principle: When any uniform, flexible cable or chain is hung between two points, gravity pulls it into a distinct, mathematically perfect curve called a catenary. Fun fact: This curve is not a parabola! The Role of Planks: Adding equally spaced weights (like wooden planks for a deck) smooths out the sag until the main cable forms the perfect curve. 2. Building the Deck The Deck: By hanging a flat surface (the road deck) from this main sagging cable using vertical hangers, the bridge deck is created. The Problem: The weight of this deck would cause the towers supporting the main cable to tilt inward. 3. The Modern Solution To stop the towers from collapsing inward, engineers added a counter-tension system: Anchorage: Cables are run from the towers and anchored deep into the ground at both ends, pulling the towers outward to counteract the inward force of the deck's weight. The Final Fix (The Stiffening Truss): Early bridges swayed in the wind. By replacing the small planks with a single, solid piece of roadway (a stiffening deck), engineers eliminated the swaying problem. Congratulations! You've just conceptually invented the modern suspension bridge. They use minimal material to span vast distances, making them ideal for deep waters and long crossings where middle piers aren't possible. 😈CONGRATS, YOU'RE AN ENGINEER! #suspensionbridge #civilengineering #bridgedesign #catenary #engineeringfacts #physics #howitworks #goldengatebridge #innovation #reels #techbehindthings #thepartyouneversee](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DRm77XGk9aZ/?utm_source=popular_topic_grid)

[[](https://www.instagram.com/snoot_adventures) snoot_adventures 13.7K ⚠️The truth about visiting Capilano Suspension Bridge Park (pet friendly park). - Although there is staff at both ends of the bridge that is supposed to monitor the amount of people on the bridge at the same time, nobody in my group felt like this was being done properly. The bridge was insane packed, and it was extremely anxiety inducing because you’re squished from all sides. There is no way to get off the bridge until the people in front of you have moved forward, so you are virtually stuck and at the mercy of the other hundred people on the bridge with you (not exaggerating). This personally made me feel very unsafe. - Although this park is technically pet friendly, I would not attempt it with a dog unless the dog is either small enough to be carried in a backpack (you will need both hands free to cross the bridge safely) or you know for a fact that your dog is comfortable walking on super shaky/wobbly surfaces where you can clearly see the drop below. I saw several terrified pet dogs being dragged by their owners - please just don’t 💔 - Because of the amount of people on the bridge at the same time, nobody is looking where they are stepping - everyone is just trying to hold on to the railings for dear life to not fall because it shakes so much. So if you have a dog with you, you’re going to have to be good at body blocking and protecting your dog so he doesn’t get trampled. People can fall on you/your dog due to how shaky the bridge is (your dog can loose balance too). For us we managed by staying in between people we knew so that at least I knew we were safe in front and behind, so I could focus on blocking the side. - The fact that this park is pet friendly also means that you may be stuck on the bridge with a random dog in your dog’s face. Unfortunately, I saw very irresponsible people bring a reactive dog (not friendly) into the park - scary stuff. - The main suspension bridge is very long, shakes like crazy, and not accessible to anyone with mobility issues or using mobility devices such as a wheelchair. There is no other way to get into the park than to cross that suspension bridge.

Title: Transportation and Parking - New Orleans Museum of Art
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7
Located at One Collins Diboll Circle in City Park, the New Orleans Museum of Art is easy to find. Arrive by car, bike, bus or streetcar. Ample free parking is available in front of NOMA on Lelong Drive or behind the Besthoff Sculpture Garden.

## By Car
### From I-10 West/Baton Rouge
Take Exit 231A toward City Park/Metairie Road.
Turn left onto City Park Ave away from Metairie Road. Continue down City Park Avenue past Canal and Delgado Community College. Turn left onto N. Carrollton Ave from City Park Avenue. Turn left at Esplanade Avenue. You are facing Lelong Drive and NOMA.

## By Car
### From I-10 East/Downtown
Take the Carrollton Ave North, Exit 232, toward US-61/Tulane Avenue. Merge onto S. Carrollton Avenue. Continue 1.6 miles. Turn left at Esplanade Avenue. You are facing Lelong Drive and NOMA.

## By Car
### Parking
Parking is always free on Lelong Drive and the streets surrounding NOMA within City Park. Handicap spaces are reserved at the front of the museum adjacent an entrance ramp. The handicap entrances are located on the left and right side of the museum near Café NOMA and the NOMA Museum Shop. Ramps at the main museum entrance stairs lead to a courtyard. Ring the buzzer on the door and security staff will allow entry. Please call 504.658.4105 if you require additional assistance.

## By Taxi or Ride Share
It will take about 15 minutes to arrive at NOMA by cab, Lyft, or Uber from the French Quarter or CBD. Click here for more information about local cab companies.

## By Bike
NOMA is less than 3 miles from downtown and the historic French Quarter. Blue Bikes—New Orleans’ community-run bikeshare—provides stations across the city. Lock up at the two conveniently located hubs near the museum at City Park and Esplanade Avenues or at Café du Monde.

## By Streetcar
The Canal–City Park streetcar lineterminates at the intersection of Wisner Avenue and Esplanade Street, within a short walking distance of NOMA and the Besthoff Sculpture Garden. Click here for the streetcar schedule.

## By Bus
Buses and streetcars are operated by the New Orleans Regional Transit Authority. RTA bus routes with stops near the museum include #27-Louisiana, #60-Hayne, #90 Carrollton, and #91 Jackson-Esplanade. Visit the RTA website for route maps and schedules.
_Visitors from across the state of Louisiana receive $3 off one adult general museum admission ticket when they show their same-day ticket or receipt fromNew Orleans Regional Transit Authoritybuses or streetcars or from theBlue Bikesrideshare network._

texts.0: Located at One Collins Diboll Circle in City Park, the New Orleans Museum of Art is easy to find. Arrive by car, bike, bus or streetcar. Ample free parking is available in front of NOMA on Lelong Drive or behind the Besthoff Sculpture Garden.
texts.1:
## By Car
### From I-10 West/Baton Rouge
Take Exit 231A toward City Park/Metairie Road.
Turn left onto City Park Ave away from Metairie Road. Continue down City Park Avenue past Canal and Delgado Community College. Turn left onto N. Carrollton Ave from City Park Avenue. Turn left at Esplanade Avenue. You are facing Lelong Drive and NOMA.
texts.2:
## By Car
### From I-10 East/Downtown
Take the Carrollton Ave North, Exit 232, toward US-61/Tulane Avenue. Merge onto S. Carrollton Avenue. Continue 1.6 miles. Turn left at Esplanade Avenue. You are facing Lelong Drive and NOMA.
texts.3:
## By Car
### Parking
Parking is always free on Lelong Drive and the streets surrounding NOMA within City Park. Handicap spaces are reserved at the front of the museum adjacent an entrance ramp. The handicap entrances are located on the left and right side of the museum near Café NOMA and the NOMA Museum Shop. Ramps at the main museum entrance stairs lead to a courtyard. Ring the buzzer on the door and security staff will allow entry. Please call 504.658.4105 if you require additional assistance.
texts.4:
## By Taxi or Ride Share
It will take about 15 minutes to arrive at NOMA by cab, Lyft, or Uber from the French Quarter or CBD. Click here for more information about local cab companies.
texts.5:
## By Bike
NOMA is less than 3 miles from downtown and the historic French Quarter. Blue Bikes—New Orleans’ community-run bikeshare—provides stations across the city. Lock up at the two conveniently located hubs near the museum at City Park and Esplanade Avenues or at Café du Monde.
texts.6:
## By Streetcar
The Canal–City Park streetcar lineterminates at the intersection of Wisner Avenue and Esplanade Street, within a short walking distance of NOMA and the Besthoff Sculpture Garden. Click here for the streetcar schedule.
texts.7:
## By Bus
Buses and streetcars are operated by the New Orleans Regional Transit Authority. RTA bus routes with stops near the museum include #27-Louisiana, #60-Hayne, #90 Carrollton, and #91 Jackson-Esplanade. Visit the RTA website for route maps and schedules.
_Visitors from across the state of Louisiana receive $3 off one adult general museum admission ticket when they show their same-day ticket or receipt fromNew Orleans Regional Transit Authoritybuses or streetcars or from theBlue Bikesrideshare network._
